title: Praise
hook: say what's good about someone out loud
tomorrow: why does a son's rehearsed speech lose its last line?

segments.voice: Yesterday, gossip: a rumor is a fire that needs wood, and it goes out when someone stops carrying it. The line was not repeated. Today, the opposite kind of talk.

A toast at a retirement party. A speech at the end-of-season banquet. A comment under a friend's post. Saying something good about someone, out loud, in front of people, can be strangely hard. Luke tells about a man who was praised twice without ever being in the room. In Capernaum, Jewish elders hurry to Jesus with a request from a Roman officer, a centurion, whose servant is dying. They plead his case, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "he loveth our nation; and he hath built us a synagogue." Jesus goes with them. Then, near the house, a second message arrives…
screen: `A TOAST, A SPEECH, A COMMENT.` → `HE BUILT US A SYNAGOGUE.` → `A SECOND MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: …from the centurion himself, carried by friends: "Lord, trouble not thyself; for I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof." Just say the word, he adds. He's a man under orders; he knows how a word works. Luke says Jesus marveled. Then he does something easy to miss. He turns around to the crowd following him and says it out loud: "Amen I say to you, I have not found so great faith, not even in Israel." The servant is healed. Look at how the praise travels. Jewish elders praise a Roman, an outsider, by naming exactly what he did. Then Jesus praises him again, in public, to a crowd that may not have expected it. Neither praise is vague. The elders could have said he's a good man; they said what he built, and for whom. Neither is flattery; the centurion isn't even there to hear it. And his own humble words stayed: Catholics echo them at Mass, just before Communion. Paul asks Christians to build one another up. Praise is one of the plainest ways to do it: the good thing you noticed, named specifically, said where others can hear.
screen: `I AM NOT WORTHY.` · `HE TURNS TO THE CROWD.` · `PRAISE THAT NAMES WHAT WAS DONE.` · `HIS WORDS, BEFORE COMMUNION.` · then, large: `SAY THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write one sentence of praise about someone you know. Make it specific, the way the elders said he built us a synagogue, not just that he's great. Start with what they did, not what they are. Read it back slowly, until it's ready to be said out loud where they, and others, can hear it.
Praise. Saying the good in someone out loud, specifically, where others can hear it, the way Jesus turned to the crowd.
Your line: say the good. The elders named what he built, and Jesus said it to the whole crowd. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Before Communion at Mass, Catholics echo the centurion's words of Luke 7:6–7, and the Church's tradition of honoring saints is, in part, praising out loud the good that people did.

fork.setup: at your cousin's graduation party, everyone toasts the graduate. your quiet uncle, who drove her to every early practice, never gets mentioned. what would Luke's story do?
options: say out loud what he did, in front of everyone.
thank him privately later so he isn't embarrassed.
toast only the graduate; it's her day, not his.
fork.reveal: Jesus didn't praise the centurion quietly; he turned to the crowd. and the elders praised by naming exactly what was done.

original.note: Latin: Lord, I am not worthy. the centurion's words, echoed before Communion.

trapdoor: what you thought: praise is something you give God, not people.
what it means: saying the good in someone out loud, specifically, where others can hear.
what a scholar hears: in Luke 7 praise crosses a border: Jewish elders praise a Roman officer, and Jesus praises his faith to the crowd.

options: Make it specific, like the elders: name what he built, and who for. Then say it.
Keep it general. Specific praise in public would just embarrass him.
Skip the praise and roast him a little. People remember funny toasts.
chat.meaning: The elders didn't say he's nice; they said he built us a synagogue, and Jesus told the crowd. Say the good, specifically, out loud.

Capernaum.meaning: a lakeside town in Galilee where Jesus taught

synagogue.meaning: a Jewish house of prayer and study

notes: Douay-Rheims Luke 7:5, 7:6 and 7:9 quoted from memory; confirm exact Challoner wording.

Luke 7:1–10 retold: elders sent by the centurion; friends sent with the second message; 'say the word' and 'I also am a man subject to authority' (7:7–8) paraphrased; Jesus marveled and turned to the multitude (7:9). Confirm.
The Mass response before Communion is described, not quoted (the current English Missal text is not public domain). Latin 'Domine, non sum dignus' is from the Vulgate/Missal. Confirm.
Unity note: the story shows Jewish elders praising a Roman officer and Jesus praising a Gentile's faith; framed as praise crossing a border, ranking no one.
Practice kind: write a line by hand. Outline practice 'praise someone publicly'.
